title: China Applies its Industrial Playbook to Brain Chips - The Wire China
gist: China is running its standard industrial-policy playbook on brain-computer interfaces: BCI was named a 'future industry' in the 15th Five-Year Plan, venture funding jumped from 1.5 billion yuan in all of 2025 to 6.47 billion yuan ($890 million) by early July 2026, and Beijing has already approved the world's first commercial invasive implant (Neuracle's NEO) plus standardized procedure pricing. Chinese firms are deliberately diverging from Neuralink toward less-invasive, ultrasound and epidural approaches with lower regulatory barriers, while remaining dependent on foreign suppliers for critical components.

insights.claim: China's latest five-year plan designates brain-computer interfaces a 'future industry' alongside fusion energy, quantum technology and embodied intelligence, giving the sector top-level political cover and subsidy access.
insights.speaker: Ella Apostoaie
insights.so_what: Designation in the five-year plan is the reliable leading indicator for a multi-year wave of Chinese state funds, local guidance funds and reimbursement support; use it to time entries in the supply chain.
insights.locator: Beijing is right behind Hu and his peers

insights.claim: Unlike the United States, where Elon Musk, Jeff Bezos and Bill Gates are the major backers of neurotech ventures, the government is the key driver of brain-computer interface development in China.
insights.speaker: Ella Apostoaie
insights.so_what: In China the policy signal precedes the capital, so state documents are a better forward indicator of BCI funding than private VC sentiment; the reverse holds in the US.
insights.locator: Unlike the U.S., where tech titans such as Musk

insights.claim: The China Brain Project, launched five years ago as a 15-year national initiative, allocated over 3 billion yuan ($443 million) to fund neuroscience research.
insights.speaker: Ella Apostoaie
insights.so_what: Establishes that the current commercial wave rests on nearly a decade of pre-funded basic research, not a standing start.
insights.locator: Five years ago, the country kickstarted the China Brain Project

insights.claim: A joint policy from the National Development and Reform Commission and six other ministries set explicit targets: accelerate BCI adoption in manufacturing, healthcare and consumer products by 2027, and build two to three globally leading enterprises by 2030.
insights.speaker: Ella Apostoaie
insights.so_what: The '2-3 national champions by 2030' formula implies deliberate consolidation — expect a small number of Chinese BCI firms to be favored with orders and listings, and the rest to be squeezed.
insights.locator: Then last July, the National Development and Reform Commission

insights.claim: Local Chinese governments have stacked dedicated BCI money on top of central policy: Shenzhen announced a 1.2 billion yuan ($165 million) brain science fund in December, Nanjing unveiled a 1 billion yuan ($148 million) BCI industry guidance fund in May, and Shanghai built a BCI industrial hub called Neuro Space that already hosts over fifty companies.
insights.speaker: Ella Apostoaie
insights.so_what: Municipal guidance funds are typically the marginal buyer in Chinese sector booms; their scale here suggests valuations in Chinese BCI will run ahead of clinical evidence.
insights.locator: Local governments have followed suit

insights.claim: Venture capital funding for Chinese brain-computer interface companies reached 6.47 billion yuan ($890 million) by early July 2026, up from just 1.5 billion yuan ($221 million) in all of 2025, according to data platform ITJuzi.
insights.speaker: Ella Apostoaie
insights.so_what: A more than fourfold funding jump in half a year is the clearest quantitative marker that Chinese BCI has entered its capital-formation phase — a window for component suppliers and a warning on late-stage entry prices.
insights.locator: And, as so often in China, private capital is following Beijing’s lead

insights.claim: Neuracle Technology, the Shanghai-based developer of the NEO implant, filed last month for an initial public offering on Shanghai's STAR market seeking to raise 2.5 billion yuan ($370 million).
insights.speaker: Ella Apostoaie
insights.so_what: A STAR listing gives the first commercially approved invasive BCI a public comparable, creating a valuation anchor for the whole Chinese neurotech cohort.
insights.locator: Last month, Neuracle filed for an initial public offering

insights.claim: BrainCo, the Hangzhou-based firm building AI neural-decoding algorithms, bionic hands and a sleep-aid headset, is aiming for an IPO in Hong Kong and is expanding into pain and weight management with what it calls a 'digital Ozempic' that suppresses appetite like GLP-1 drugs.
insights.speaker: Ella Apostoaie
insights.so_what: A neurotech device positioned as a GLP-1 substitute is a direct, under-priced competitive vector against obesity-drug franchises; watch for clinical data and Hong Kong listing filings.
insights.locator: Another company, BrainCo, is aiming for an IPO in Hong Kong

insights.claim: Gestala, a Chengdu-based BCI startup founded in January 2026, has already raised $84 million across two rounds from Hongshan and Kaifu Lee's Sinovation Ventures.
insights.speaker: Ella Apostoaie
insights.so_what: $84 million into a six-month-old company signals top-tier Chinese VCs treating ultrasound BCI as a land-grab, not an experiment.
insights.locator: Gestala, a Chengdu-based startup founded in January

insights.claim: Unlike Neuralink, which plants electrodes into the brain's cortex to target individual neurons, most Chinese companies are exploring less invasive approaches — a deliberate divergence in technical strategy rather than a lag.
insights.speaker: Ella Apostoaie
insights.so_what: The competitive race is not head-to-head on the same product; less-invasive platforms address a far larger addressable market with cheaper regulatory paths, so market-share comparisons based on Neuralink's roadmap will mislead.
insights.locator: As Simon-Kucher’s Liu points out

insights.claim: Ultrasound-based brain reading is easier to commercialize than electrode implants because it requires no surgical procedure and therefore faces lower regulatory barriers globally, and it can capture signals from a larger part of the brain — the same approach Sam Altman's Merge Labs is pursuing.
insights.speaker: Ella Apostoaie
insights.so_what: Two well-funded camps on opposite sides of the Pacific converging on ultrasound marks it as the consensus non-invasive bet; regulatory arbitrage means it can reach revenue years before implant players.
insights.locator: Phoenix Peng, co-founder of Gestala, says using ultrasound

insights.claim: The technology gap between Chinese companies and Neuralink in conventional electric BCI has shrunk from eight years to four within the last few years, and is even narrower in ultrasound, according to Gestala co-founder Phoenix Peng, who also co-founded NeuroXess in 2021.
insights.speaker: Ella Apostoaie
insights.so_what: If the four-year gap is real, US neurotech's technical moat is thinner than its funding lead implies — relevant to export-control debates and to any assumption of durable Western pricing power.
insights.quote: I am very confident that in the next two years or so, we can transition from a follower to a leader in the ultrasound BCI track
insights.locator: Peng, who also co-founded NeuroXess in 2021

insights.claim: Billionaire BCI funder Chen Tianqiao argues the technology has made no massive leaps and that the capabilities exciting investors now were already mature a decade ago, reckoning Chinese companies will soon find it 'very easy' to surpass Neuralink.
insights.speaker: Ella Apostoaie
insights.so_what: A contrarian read that the bottleneck is commercialization and reimbursement, not physics — implies the winners will be decided by regulatory and payer access, not lab breakthroughs.
insights.quote: The things everyone is so excited about now were already mature a decade ago.
insights.locator: “Honestly, the technology hasn’t made any massive leaps,”

insights.claim: Non-invasive BCI's core engineering constraint is signal-to-noise: extracting clean, reliable neural signals through hair, skin and bone remains unsolved, which is why AI decoding algorithms must be constantly retrained per patient condition.
insights.speaker: Ella Apostoaie
insights.so_what: The value in non-invasive BCI accrues to whoever owns the decoding models and patient data, not the headset hardware — a software-margin business hiding inside a device story.
insights.quote: Reading through the skull means extracting the faintest neural signals from an enormous background of noise
insights.locator: Non-invasive methods may be safer, but there are tradeoffs

insights.claim: BrainCo frames Neuralink as serving a narrow patient group requiring direct neural intervention while positioning itself for the mass market where non-invasive methods work without surgical risk 'at a fraction of the cost.'
insights.speaker: Ella Apostoaie
insights.so_what: Explicit market segmentation: the volume opportunity is consumer-adjacent and price-led, which favors Chinese manufacturing cost structures.
insights.quote: We’re building for the vast majority of applications, where non-invasive methods deliver meaningful outcomes without surgical risk, at a fraction of the cost.
insights.locator: “Neuralink is opening an important door

insights.claim: A typical BCI clinical trial in China costs about one-fifth of the equivalent in the United States, driven by lower overhead and labour costs plus a greater pool of patients and animals.
insights.speaker: Ella Apostoaie
insights.so_what: The same 5x trial-cost differential that reshaped biotech licensing is now present in neurotech — expect Western firms to in-license Chinese BCI clinical assets.
insights.locator: As in biotech, a typical BCI clinical trial in China

insights.claim: A Chinese BCI startup can complete fundraising and build its factory, lab and animal facility within six months, a build cycle its founder calls impossible in the US or Europe.
insights.speaker: Ella Apostoaie
insights.so_what: Time-to-capacity, not capital, is the decisive competitive variable; Western incumbents lose optionality every quarter they spend on permitting and site build.
insights.quote: We could finish fundraising, and build our factory, our lab, and our animal facility all within six months
insights.locator: “We could finish fundraising, and build our factory

insights.claim: NeuroXess is set to begin mass production later this year, building a Jiangxi factory that will churn out 10,000 sets of brain chips annually, targeting some 3 million Chinese patients with spinal cord injuries.
insights.speaker: Ella Apostoaie
insights.so_what: Stated annual unit capacity of 10,000 implants moves BCI from clinical curiosity to a volume manufacturing supply chain — relevant to electrode, packaging and encapsulation suppliers.
insights.locator: The maker of the chips is NeuroXess

insights.claim: NeuroXess's founder characterizes the sector as moving out of proof-of-concept into a 'full-scale industrial explosion,' with roughly 200 Chinese companies now in the nascent BCI sector.
insights.speaker: Ella Apostoaie
insights.so_what: 200 entrants against a policy target of 2-3 national champions implies a violent shakeout — favor picks-and-shovels exposure over single-name equity bets.
insights.quote: The industry is transitioning from a ‘proof-of-concept’ stage into a full-scale industrial explosion,
insights.locator: “The industry is transitioning from a ‘proof-of-concept’ stage

insights.claim: In March 2026 China became the first country to approve commercial use of an invasive BCI system — NEO, a coin-sized wireless implant from Neuracle Technology and Tsinghua University researchers that sits atop the brain's protective membrane — after clinical trials on 32 patients, with the first commercial surgery completed in Shanghai.
insights.speaker: Ella Apostoaie
insights.so_what: First-in-world commercial approval means Chinese firms will accumulate real-world implant data ahead of US competitors, compounding into a regulatory and evidence lead.
insights.locator: Regulators have also expedited their reviews

insights.claim: By the end of last year 62 medical institutions across China had launched BCI centers and clinics, with the latest opening at Lhasa People's Hospital in Tibet.
insights.speaker: Ella Apostoaie
insights.so_what: Clinical-channel build-out is the hard part of medtech scaling; 62 centers is distribution infrastructure that Western entrants cannot replicate quickly in China.
insights.locator: China is rapidly building the infrastructure

insights.claim: Beijing's municipal government has set a standardized price of 7,980 yuan ($1,200) for an invasive BCI implantation with partial insurance coverage for urban employees, while a Shanghai-backed commercial scheme covers up to 150,000 yuan ($21,450) of total cost.
insights.speaker: Ella Apostoaie
insights.so_what: A $1,200 administered price for the procedure caps revenue per patient dramatically versus US expectations — model Chinese BCI as a volume, low-ASP business.
insights.locator: Beijing’s municipal government, for instance, has taken the lead

insights.claim: The binding commercial constraint on BCI in both the US and China is payer coverage: insurers wary of new technology can take years to reimburse, a lag the medical industry calls the 'valley of death,' and most Chinese patients still pay out of pocket.
insights.speaker: Ella Apostoaie
insights.so_what: Reimbursement decisions, not device approvals, are the revenue-inflection catalyst to watch for every listed BCI name.
insights.locator: The next step is figuring out how to pay for BCI treatments

themes.theme: Demand drivers, bottlenecks and talent flows

insights.claim: Some 2.8 million patients in China suffered from spinal cord injuries in 2021, and Beijing's interest in BCI is being driven as much by its aging population's enormous future medical needs as by technology rivalry — with BCI framed as a way to reduce patient reliance on the public health system.
insights.speaker: Ella Apostoaie
insights.so_what: Framing BCI as fiscal relief for an aging state health system, not just prestige tech, makes sustained state procurement far more likely than in a pure geopolitical-race narrative.
insights.locator: But experts say Beijing is also becoming keener on BCI

insights.claim: The Chinese BCI industry still depends on foreign suppliers for critical components and lacks interdisciplinary talent spanning neuroscience, electronic engineering and clinical medicine, according to Chinese healthcare research firm VC Beat.
insights.speaker: Ella Apostoaie
insights.so_what: A named foreign-component dependency in a sector Beijing has made a national priority is both an export-control pressure point and a revenue opportunity for Western specialty suppliers.
insights.locator: The Chinese BCI industry also depends on foreign suppliers

insights.claim: Bashar Badran, a former clinical lead at Neuralink, relocated from San Francisco to Chengdu in April to become head of clinical research at Gestala — evidence of senior neurotech talent flowing from the US to China.
insights.speaker: Ella Apostoaie
insights.so_what: Reverse brain drain at the clinical-lead level compresses the capability gap faster than capital alone and is a signal worth tracking across frontier-tech sectors.
insights.locator: In April, Bashar Badran, a former clinical lead at Neuralink

insights.claim: Austin-based BCI startup Paradronomics publicly warned in March that the US has one approved BCI product while China has a national industrial strategy, a diverse competitor pipeline beyond NEO, and reimbursement infrastructure already forming — attributing China's position to top-down, long-horizon coordination.
insights.speaker: Ella Apostoaie
insights.so_what: A US competitor conceding the structural advantage is a credible signal that policy support, not technology, is the decisive variable — and a lobbying tailwind for US neurotech industrial policy.
insights.quote: Whereas the U.S. has one approved BCI product, China has a national industrial strategy, a diverse pipeline of competitors spanning far beyond just NEO, and reimbursement infrastructure already taking shape around them
insights.locator: In March, Paradronomics, an Austin-based BCI startup

insights.claim: Chinese BCI capability is already at the level of two paralyzed patients 800 kilometers apart playing live chess — one lifting pieces via an exoskeleton glove, the other directing a robot by thought — using NeuroXess chips implanted on the brain surface.
insights.speaker: Ella Apostoaie
insights.so_what: A concrete, networked two-patient demonstration is the kind of proof point that pulls forward payer and regulator willingness, and it is happening in China first.
insights.locator: Last month, two men played a live game of chess

insights.claim: Beyond medicine, Chinese planners see BCI potential in defense and cognitive augmentation — devices intended to enhance human memory, focus and intelligence.
insights.speaker: Ella Apostoaie
insights.so_what: A defense and augmentation angle raises the probability of US export controls and investment screening on neurotech components and IP.
insights.locator: The frontier technology also has potential in areas like defense
